extracted.intended_audience: general U.S. newspaper readers; journalists and editors covering wartime news and public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of Associated Press wartime and domestic news dispatches (June 1943) covering military actions, government hearings, censorship debates, and home-front issues; useful as examples of news reporting practice during WWII.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper wartime censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: “Proper censorship which covers both the sins of omission and commission is a buckler in time of national peril.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Palmer Hoyt argues that censorship must be balanced (not only omission but commission), and that unwisely applied censorship can debilitate journalism. The page warns against overly broad or poorly applied censorship that confuses rather than protects the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, streamlined clearance chain for stories
rubrics_metrics.description: There is confusion as to who should be contacted to clear a particular story; the present system 'filters down through military, naval and civilian authorities, many of whom are unfamiliar with the wartime censorship code.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights a practical difficulty: multiple layers of authorities unfamiliar with the code create red tape. Implicit criterion: clearance procedures should be centralized/clarified and those responsible should be trained so news can be cleared efficiently and consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness — publish facts while they are news
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper must move quickly to publish facts while they are news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoyt emphasizes that the unwinding of departmental red tape is particularly distressing to trained newspaper workers; delays caused by slow clearance impede the essential journalistic duty to report timely facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overcautious withholding by military/naval censors
rubrics_metrics.description: Military and naval commanders in the field have demonstrated a most understandable reticence about clearing stories, and officers often 'err on the side of extreme caution and unnecessarily' withhold material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece criticizes an excessive 'err on the side of caution' approach, implying the criterion that censors should not block publication out of undue fear when withholding is not necessary for security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect war production and home-front morale when censoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship aims to prevent publication that would interfere with war production and to break down home-front morale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article and related reporting show that one accepted ground for withholding or modifying information is risk of harming war production or damaging public morale; this is presented as a legitimate boundary for wartime press restrictions.
